pilot.summary: Three-player pod at Tom Beloy's — Alex on mono-red Tannuk, Tom on Merfolk. Alex resolved Blood Moon on turn two or three and every nonbasic became a Mountain, so Smothering Tithe and everything multicoloured were uncastable and I was down to the all-red dragons. I got there with Moltensteel Dragon at the end, paying sixteen life to pump it and hitting Alex for twelve. I am not building around Blood Moon; the lesson I took was to have the mana base audited holistically.

Five-player pod at Oliver's, seat 4, and the first game on the new land base after raising it 31 to 36 that same day. It did not help — mulliganed once, sat on four or five lands on turns six and seven while Alex was tapping for twelve on turns four and five, and the cost reducer got removed so the discount engine never did its job. After that it was repeated wipes: board established, board erased. I won by staying off the radar and closing at the end, and my own read is that the deck did not win, the table's attrition did.

Game 2 of three at Oliver's, five-player pod, and the first validation game for the refactor. The mana worked — turn-one land into Sol Ring and Arcane Signet, turn-two Bloom Tender — and I curved into Miirym, Gadrak and Terror of the Peaks. Then I played Gadrak a turn too early and telegraphed the whole thing: the table read "Sean is swinging for 28 in the air" and converged, Tom killing all three artifacts so Gadrak could not activate, Alex fighting the dragons with his fight deck, Ryan removing more. Loss, and the lesson written down was speed without protection or politics makes me the obvious kill target before I can close.

Four-player pod at my house — Stuart on an Animar precon, Steven on CC Weather, David on Squirrels. I sacked a land to tutor, found Terror of the Peaks, and after that every dragon ETB was about ten targeted damage across three targets, which I used as spot removal to take out two commanders. Then I telegraphed again: the treasure pile plus fireballing every ETB made me the obvious problem, David called it out, and three players picked me apart inside one rotation. Steven flew under the radar with his tap/untap engine and won it — a political loss, not a deck loss.

Five-player pod at Oliver's; I arrived late, missed game one, and Oliver won every game that night. I was going to play Heliod and swapped to Ur-Dragon because the table said "creatures". No green source all game, so Farseek and the green dragons sat in hand, and Enlightened Tutor went for Sol Ring when it should have found a green rock or a signet. Firespitter Whelp with Twinflame Tyrant and Panharmonicon was pinging and doubling, but I cast Twinflame before the big dragons were down and it was removed immediately — the same too-early pattern, no treasure engine online at any point, and no counterspells left to answer any of it.

Three-player at my house — Stephen on Sisay, Weatherlight Captain, which is getting bonkers now that he sequences it right, and Stuart on a new Rot-Cleaver zombie deck with decayed chump blockers. I kept three lands, Arcane Signet, Smaug the Magnificent and Thrakkus the Butcher, never found the land to cast either dragon on time, and I do not stand by the keep. When The Ur-Dragon landed and Stephen targeted it, Bloom Tender was untapped with all five colours out — five mana, not two or three — and Return of the Wildspeaker was in hand for ten cards off the dragon; I did not pause, did not tap Tender, and let the removal resolve. Stephen killed Stuart through everything and had me at five, then swung with everything and left himself open at five with no blockers, so I untapped, swung with the dorks plus the two Spirit tokens Forbidden Orchard had given me, and squeaked out the win by not being too loud.

read.what_it_does: It ramps early, buys the dragons down and turns every arrival into targeted damage. Terror of the Peaks is the card the games keep coming back to: about ten damage spread across three targets on each ETB, used as spot removal, and it killed two commanders in one game (004). That confirms what the manual says the damage leg is; what the games add is that across six logged games the dragons have not closed one. Both wins came from off the radar — last seat standing after four players ground each other down (002, on V2), and a swing with the dorks and two Spirit tokens into Stephen after he swung out and left himself open at five (006).
read.how_it_plays: Fast and loud when the mana cooperates: turn-one Sol Ring and Arcane Signet, turn-two Bloom Tender (003, on V3, the first game the mana worked), and "more consistent than it has ever been" with treasure accumulating (004). The board is legible from across the table — the tells are the treasure pile and the fireball on every ETB (004) — and the pod reads lethal in the air before it is presentable and converges: Tom killing all three artifacts so Gadrak could not activate, Alex fighting the dragons, Ryan removing more (003); three players picking the deck apart inside one rotation (004). Every table it has sat at runs heavy removal — creature removal and wipes at Oliver's (002, 003), counters and targeted removal from Stephen and wipes from Stuart at home (006). Where it ends up: dead to a converged table (003, 004), stuck behind a missing colour or a land that never came (005, 006), or last seat standing by being quiet (002, 006). The one win on the current list came from not being too loud, and his first lesson from it is dorks first (006).
mindful_of: The board goes down too early, three games running on the loud line: Gadrak a turn ahead of the payoff (003, on V3); every ETB fireballed and the treasure stacked in plain sight (004); Twinflame Tyrant cast before the big dragons were down, and removed immediately (005). Sean named the cause himself — he does not like having unspent mana (005). The fix he wrote down is to drop the tempo a turn or two, and the one win on this list came from not being too loud: dorks first, stay quiet, telegraph less (006).

Pause before resolution. The Ur-Dragon landed, Stephen targeted it, Bloom Tender was untapped with all five colours out and Return of the Wildspeaker was in hand for ten cards off the dragon — and the removal resolved with no response (006). His own rule: when removal is coming in or the commander is under threat, stop and scan instant-speed responses, dorks that can tap, and cards in hand before the stack closes.
Bloom Tender is five mana once all five colours are out, not two or three. He read it low with the commander on the table, with Delighted Halfling and the other sources sitting there too (006).

There are no responses in the 99. Since the refactor pulled the counterspells there is nothing to protect a dragon or answer the converge, and both notes since say so: "I cut protection and counters for speed, and it showed" (003, on V3), "I now have zero responses" (005).

Politics is the recorded cause of two losses (003, 004). In 004 the quiet assembler won it — Steven's tap/untap engine went unanswered while the table was busy with the dragons. The standing lesson is to manage his own optics and to point the table at the quiet seat before it is unanswerable.

Two keeps he does not stand by, and two proposed mulligan rules. No green source all game in 005, with Farseek and the green-needing dragons stranded in hand even though Delighted Halfling, Birds of Paradise and Bloom Tender are all in the 99 — his rule: no green source, consider shipping it. Three lands, Arcane Signet, Smaug and Thrakkus in 006, and the land to cast either never came — "that was a hand to ship".
Tutors get spent on speed instead of on the problem in front of him — Enlightened Tutor found Sol Ring when the game was a fixing game (005).

The pod at Oliver's runs heavy creature removal and board wipes, and this deck made nothing on the way down: board established, board erased, repeat, with the cost reducer removed so the discount engine never fired (002, on V2). The removal half has not changed — 003 and 004 are the table taking the board apart, and at home Stephen's Sisay is now a tutor on a stick for any legendary piece, sequenced right, behind counters and targeted removal (006).
Deck choice can be its own problem. He swapped off Heliod to Ur-Dragon because the table said "creatures" (005), and his own view — Oliver disagrees — is that mismatched decks make salt.
Temperament. He wanted to scoop in 005, took a breath and played it out. The rule he set for himself is to stay on the field and get even inside the game.
read.what_changed: Three changes in four versions, and nothing has moved since V4 — 004, 005 and 006 were all played on it. V1 was 31 lands; after the Blood Moon game (001) the ask was a holistic mana audit, and V2 raised the count to 36, made the day of the next game. It did not show up: the first game on the new base was still four or five lands on turns six and seven while the table was on eight to ten plus dorks (002). V3 — the eminence-v3 merge — swapped density toward dorks and rocks, and that one landed: "The mana worked" (003). The same merge pulled every counterspell — Counterspell, Dovin's Veto, Swan Song — and the deck has had zero responses since (003, 005). It also cut Smothering Tithe and Moltensteel Dragon, so the card-level half of 001 is superseded: that was true of a list this deck no longer runs, and only its mana-base finding still applies. V4 was two proxy duals becoming budget lands, and the three games on it say the mana trouble that remains is not land count: no green source at all in 005, and in 006 the land to cast Smaug or Thrakkus never came, on a keep he does not stand by.
